triples.subject: Classification of diseases
triples.source_sentence: Major diseases of trees can be classified in various ways depending on the purpose to be served.

triples.subject: non-infectious or non-parasitic or physiological disease
triples.source_sentence: These are the diseases caused by non-living environment which may include poor or shallow soil dept, nutrient defiency, high temperature etc.

triples.subject: infectious or pathogenic disease
triples.source_sentence: These are the diseases caused by other living organisms. These are fungi, (the most important disease pathogens in forestry), bacteria and viruses.

triples.subject: necrotic disease
triples.source_sentence: Necrotic symptoms These are the evidence of necrosis or death of affected tissue resulting in marked change of colour from yellowing through browning to graying when the tissue finally dies. Examples of this are leaf blight, bud blight, stem canker to mention a few.

triples.subject: atrophic disease
triples.source_sentence: Atrophic: This is the slowing down in development of the affected plants parts resulting from subnormal cell division (hypoplasia). Dwarfing or stunted growth is an example. The causes could include; unfavourable environmental conditions, unfavourable soil condition, excess or deficiency of certain mineral elements.

entities.name: root or butt or collar rot

triples.subject: Hypertrophic
triples.source_sentence: This is an overgrowth of all kinds which results from abnormal cell increase (excessive cell division). The evidences are the formation of galls or tumors, witches brooms, hairy roots, leaf curls and deformation of fruits and flowers.

triples.subject: damping off
triples.source_sentence: Root diseases: As the name implies, they attack the root of trees. Examples include; damping off, root or butt or collar rot etc.

triples.source_sentence: Water logging also prevents roots from getting oxygen necessary for their development from the soil air. This may result in the death of the roots.

triples.source_sentence: In the nurseries, excessive watering of beds may lead to seedling inundation.

triples.subject: Retarded growth
triples.source_sentence: A shortage of water preventing trees from carrying out normal physical functions results in diseases. This is of importance in the arid and semi-arid forest regions.

triples.subject: Damping off
triples.source_sentence: In the nursery, the seedlings killed by drought are scattered throughout the seedbeds whereas those killed by damping off or other fungal diseases usually occur in definite groups.

triples.subject: Weakly parasitic fungi
triples.source_sentence: In the plantation, drought is brought about by periods of subnormal precipitation and drying winds eg. harmattan. Unfortunately, foresters have no control over such natural disasters. Drought injury is difficult to diagnose because the affected trees frequently succumb to weakly parasitic fungi or insects eg. termites.

It is important to avoid areas where flooding can occur and if possible the area should be close to the budded stumps (either on the beds or polybags are to be planted).

triples.subject: soil_texture

triples.subject: soil_moisture
triples.source_sentence: If cultivation is done too late when the soil moisture is high, the puddled soil may result in excessive run-off leading to soil Erosion.

triples.subject: spacing

triples.subject: spacing

triples.subject: variety_cultivars

triples.subject: First Thinning

triples.subject: Polybag Nursery Method
triples.source_sentence: Planting materials in polybags provides optimum degree of selectivity and polybagged stumps achieve much greater uniformity in growth at field planting.

triples.subject: Budding
triples.source_sentence: In Nigeria, budding is done in the wet season, commencing from the late April and extends to mid-October. However the best periods to bud are: (i) Early May until mid-July (ii) Mid September until mid October (dormant budding)

triples.subject: Budding
triples.source_sentence: In order to achieve the best results, the following should strictly be observed: 1. Do not bud in the rain when the materials are wet. Diseases are easily be transferred with wet materials. 2. Avoid budding during the dry season unless some form of irrigation or adequate watering is ensured. 3. Delay commencement of budding operations until the morning mists have subsided. This is to provide a dry surface on the budding materials. 4. Ensure that rootstocks attain a minimum diameter of 5cm and are vigorous. 5. Avoid budding to old or very large rootstock. The barks of old or large rootstock are inclined to split.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: Bud grafting requires skill which, can be acquired through constant practice.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: Poor budding can be costly as time, energy and resources are wasted when there are budding failures.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: Steps in Budding:

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: 1. Wipe and dry dirt from the ground level 15cm of rootstock.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: 2. Make two vertical cuts, of about 2cm each of 0.75cm apart and allow the excluding latex from the cut to coagulate.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: 3. Prepare the bud patch by cutting from the budwood a strip of bark wood about 2cm long and 0.75cm wide, ensuring there is a bud and a leaf scar.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: 4. Gently raise the flap open and insert the bud patch with the leaf scar below the bud. Ensure that the bud patch is in the centre and there is minimal space remaining on the either side.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: 5. Press the flap back over the bud and bound in place with waterproof materials such as budding tapes or polyethylene plastic film.

triples.subject: Bud grafting
triples.source_sentence: The tapes should be removed after about 3 weeks. In doing this gradually remove both tapes and twine. Cut off the flap at the bottom or top to reveal the graft. This is re-examined after about 7-10 days for green tissue on the patch. If green tissue is revealed with a gentle scratch, the patch has been successful.

triples.subject: Budwood
triples.source_sentence: In a nursery programme, it is important to ensure that there is an available supply of bud wood. This can be in the form of conventional brown bud wood or green bud sticks.

triples.subject: Budwood
triples.source_sentence: Bud wood nursery should be done one year in advance of preparing a field nursery so that an optimum supply of buds will be available for grafting.

triples.source_sentence: Purchase and planting of budded stumps of preferred clones from a reliable source. Ensuring that each clone is well demarcated, if more than one clone is purchased.

triples.subject: Trees

triples.subject: Stumping_and_burning

triples.source_sentence: In Nigeria, substantial research effort had been given to Beniseed dehulling, development of suitable oil extraction methods, protein enrichment of food using the press cake (in infant weaning foods) and on the design/fabrication of processing machines at the Federal Institute of industrial Research (FIRO), Oshodi. The development of appropriate processing and utilization technologies had also received some research attention at NCRI. For example, it had been demonstrated that dehulling of Beniseed becomes easier with the use of 0,1N or 0.01N sodium hydroxide solution compared to dry, cold or hot water method. A prototype 10kg/batch Beniseed oil-extractor has also been designed and fabricated. Several Beniseed recipes and snacks have been developed in line with local food habits and preferences.

triples.source_sentence: Under continuous cultivation, apply 300 kg (6 bags) of NPK 25:10:10, 10:10/ha, at planting as band or broadcast application, to give 75 kg N, 30 kg P2O5, and 30 kg K2O/ha.

triples.subject: Fertilizer_Rate_and_Time_of_Application
triples.source_sentence: Apply 400 kg (8 bags) of 25:10:10, 100 kg (2 bags) of single superphosphate and 3 - 5kg of zinc sulphate per hectare at planting as band or broadcast to give a total of 100 kg N, 58 kg P2O6, 40 kg K2O, 14 kg S, and 1 - 2kg Zn/ha.

triples.subject: Fertilizer_Rate_and_Time_of_Application
triples.source_sentence: Stem borer attack should be controlled by applying 1.68 kg active ingredient of Vetox 85/ha, i.e., 3 standard match box filled to the level per 4.5 liters (1 gal.) of water. Two applications, the first at 2 weeks after planting, and the second 2 weeks after.

triples.subject: Fertilizer_Rate_and_Time_of_Application

triples.source_sentence: Cool, wet weather encourages many pathogens that cause seedling diseases and kernel rots.

triples.source_sentence: The plant spacing recommended for maize in the Nigerian savannas is 75 x 50 cm, where 2 plants per stand are adopted (Fig. 7).

triples.subject: Seed_rate
triples.source_sentence: About 15 - 20 kg of maize seeds is required to plant a hectare, which is about 2 acres.

triples.subject: Striga
triples.source_sentence: In many parts of the Nigerian savannas, Striga is a notorious parasitic weed that has continuously posed a great threat to maize production.

triples.subject: Striga
triples.source_sentence: Under severe infestation, even before the emergence of Striga, the maize plants are usually severely attacked and look yellowish, stunted, and wilting.

triples.subject: chemical_weed_control

triples.subject: Herbicide
triples.source_sentence: The sprayer should be calibrated each time herbicides are to be applied in order to enhance efficacy.

triples.subject: Seeds
triples.source_sentence: Dressing the seeds prior to planting easily controls most of the diseases (whether soil-or seed-borne).

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: During harvest, the cobs can be broken by hand from the plant or the whole plant can be cut with a cutlass (Fig. 9). Where the entire plants are harvested, they are often stacked in the field to allow the grain to dry further.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: In the humid zones, the crop can be dried in a traditional ventilated granary.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: When maize is to be consumed fresh, harvesting should be conducted when the silk has turned brown (50 - 70 days after planting).

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: But when grain is needed, harvest as soon as the grain is dry enough (80 - 110 days after planting) depending on the variety.

triples.subject: Yield
triples.source_sentence: The average yield of maize in Northern Nigeria is about 2500 - 3500 kg/ha of threshed grain using recommended fertilizers, varieties, seed-dressing, and improved cultural practices.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: Maize meant for future use should be dried to 10 - 12% moisture content and properly stored.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: The store or granary should be very clean before and during storage. This is aimed at preventing the loss of grain due to storage pests.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: For slightly larger scale production, they will harvest the crop when it is reasonably dry and then store it in freely ventilated stores or granaries that allow air to pass through the crop and continue the drying process.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: In small-scale production, farmers store quantities over fireplaces and on the roofs of houses.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: In small-scale production, farmers store quantities over fireplaces and on the roofs of houses.

triples.subject: Maize
triples.source_sentence: Maize that will be stored for 6 months or more should, in addition to hygiene in the store, be treated with phostoxin

triples.subject: grain weevils (Sitophilus spp. and Tribolium spp.)
triples.source_sentence: Infestation may be by insects already present where maize grain had previously been stored, or by cross-infestation between stores, or by cross-infestation between granaries during storage.

triples.subject: grain weevils (Sitophilus spp. and Tribolium spp.)
triples.source_sentence: In some cases, an infestation may start on the field, especially when maize is left for too long before being harvested.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: Phostoxin tablets or pellets may be used to store more maize in an airtight container or large storage in sacks.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: Large-scale storage in bags such as pyramids will require a complete cover with tarpaulin after application with 4 - 6 tablets or pellets per ton, (wrapped in newspaper) in some of the bags.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: For bagged produce, the rate is 1-2 tablets per 100 kg grain sack.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: The tablet is wrapped in small tissue paper and placed in the middle of the sack.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: Also, grains must be properly dried; below 12 percent moisture level before storage to avoid mold. Clean granaries and stores before filling with new grains.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: For fumigants to be effective, they must be applied where there is air-tight storage condition in sacks, containers or buildings.

triples.subject: Phostoxin
triples.source_sentence: Large-scale storage in bags such as pyramids will require a complete cover with tarpaulin after application with 4 - 6 tablets or pellets per ton, (wrapped in newspaper) in some of the bags.

In the early 1970s the "T" strain caused severe damage to maize cultivars in which the Texas source of male sterility had been incorporated. triples.subject: Stenocarpella ear rot
triples.source_sentence: Stenocarpella ear rots are commonly found in hot, humid maize-growing areas.

triples.subject: Stenocarpella ear rot
triples.source_sentence: Maize ears show characteristic development of irregular bleached areas on husks. These areas enlarge until the husks become completely dried, although the plant is still green.

triples.subject: Stenocarpella ear rot
triples.source_sentence: If husks are removed, ears appear chaffy and bleached, with a white, cottony growth between the kernels (Photo 78). Late in the season, many small, black pycnidia form on kernels and cob tissues (Photo 79).

triples.subject: Stenocarpella ear rot
triples.source_sentence: Severely infected ears are very light. Infection more frequently occurs through the shank and moves from the cob to the kernels. Stem borer injury in the ear often increases incidence of this disease.

triples.subject: Stenocarpella ear rot
triples.source_sentence: Stenocarpella maydis produces the mycotoxin diplodiatoxin and S. macrospora produces diplodiol, both harmful to birds.

triples.source_sentence: Till the land to bury and kill the disease.

triples.subject: plant_crops_away_from_fields_with_disease
triples.source_sentence: Plant crops away from, and upwind of, fields with the disease as it can travel by wind.

triples.subject: grow_legume_cover_crops
triples.source_sentence: If direct seeding (no-tillage or zero tillage), grow legume cover crops before planting, e.g. lablab, velvet bean or sunhemp. Clear the legume just before planting the maize by making furrows without cultivating the land.

triples.subject: avoid_overhead_irrigation
triples.source_sentence: Avoid overhead irrigation, if possible, as wet plants can encourage disease development.

triples.subject: rotate_crop
triples.source_sentence: Rotate crop at least every 1-2 years. The disease only infects maize, so other crops in the rotation will not become infected.

triples.subject: use_fertilizer_moderately
triples.source_sentence: Use fertilizer moderately. High levels of nitrogen in the soil has been associated with increased disease severity.

triples.subject: check_crop
triples.source_sentence: Regularly check crop, especially when full canopy has developed, as the resulting high relative humidity in the canopy encourages disease development.

triples.subject: high_humidity
triples.source_sentence: Favourable conditions for disease development include high humidity and temperatures between 22 and 30 deg C.

triples.subject: temperatures_between_22_and_30_deg_C

triples.subject: plough_in_or_collect_and_burn_crop_debris
triples.source_sentence: After harvest, plough in or collect and burn crop debris. This is very important as the fungus can survive on the leaves and stalks from one season to another.

triples.subject: MSD
triples.source_sentence: Breeding programs at IITA and several organizations in the past 50 years have developed and released several MSD-resistant varieties. Resistance to MSD is considered an essential adaptive trait, and breeding programs have been incorporating it continuously in their development of new varieties intended for release in Africa. The conventional system of incorporating resistance involves crossing the best plants with the most desirable traits, such as high yield, disease resistance, and other farmer preferred characters. Screening of early generation lines for recovery resistance to MSV using viruliferous leafhoppers in screenhouse and eld may take more than ve to seven years to nally develop a variety that has acceptable levels of resistance [9].

triples.subject: MSD
triples.source_sentence: Development and use of markers for selection in crop improvement have become a useful technique for breeders. Since the MSD resistance trait has high heritability, controlled by a few genes [11 - 13], the application of markers in transferring genes for resistance can be easier and quicker than the conventional selection using phenotyping. Molecular markers can help breeders select individuals carrying target genes in a segregating population based on patterns of tightly linked markers with due regard to their phenotypes. The quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for resistance to MSD in maize have been identi ed and mapped. Kyetere et al. [14] identi ed a major gene on chromosome 1 (Msv1) in Tzi4, a tolerant line from IITA. Welz et al. [13] detected a major QTL on chromosome 1 and minor QTLs on chromosomes 2, 3, and 4. The presence of a major QTL for resistance to MSD on the short arm of chromosome 1 has been identi ed in diverse germplasm and across environments [11 - 16]. Nair et al. [17] mapped Msv1 and identi ed 19 SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphism) in the region between 82 and 93 Mb on chromosome 1. Three SNPs (snpZM0020-PZE-101093951, SnpZM0021-PZE-0186065237, and snpZM0021-PZE0186365075) were identi ed in the haplotype block at 87 Mb on chromosome 1 and found an accuracy of 0.94 in predicting Msv1 QTL in maize lines [17]. High-throughput kompetitive allele speci c PCR assays (KASP) have been developed for these three SNPs as potential breeder-ready markers for the indirect selection of MSV resistance in breeding pipelines.

triples.source_sentence: Induced mutagenesis has been effectively used in crop breeding to create new genetic variability by introducing stable and heritable mutations in the plant genome (Wanga et al., 2020; Dossa et al., 2023). This creates new valuable traits that can be incorporated into well-adapted cultivars. Unlike natural genetic variation, which occurs at a low frequency (10 5 to 10 8 per locus), induced mutagenesis can increase genetic variation by 1000 to a million times, making it a crucial strategy for genetic enhancement in crop breeding programs (FAO/IAEA Mutant Varieties Database; Jiang and Ramachandran, 2010; Wanga et al., 2020). Mutation breeding has improved MSV resistance, grain yield, and agronomic traits in maize.

triples.subject: yellowish brown moths with spots on their wings
triples.source_sentence: The stem borer makes a tunnel inside the stem. Sometimes the tunnel goes as far as the ear. The maize leaves turn yellow and the stem gradually rots. When crops are damaged a strong wind can blow them over. Background The borer eats and grows for three to five weeks. The borer hatches from eggs which are laid by yellowish brown moths with spots on their wings. The moth lays eggs in clusters in the leaf sheath. The stem borer lives in the dead stalk and stubble from one year to the next.

triples.subject: Cassava green mite
triples.source_sentence: The cassava green mite biological control campaign has resulted in a similar continent-wide success, largely through the establishment of Brazilian populations of the predatory mite Z. aripo. This predator is now established in at least 20 countries in sub-Saharan Africa (Hanna and Toko, 2003; Yaninek and Hanna,2003). Repeated surveys in at least 12 countries and a total of 18 predator exclusion trials have shown that the predators have reduced cassava green mite densities by 60oh and increased cassava root yield up to 80% depending on location and cassava variety (Yaninek and Hanna 2003; Hanna et a\.2005), and notably without any negative non-target effects (Zannou et a|.2007).Fot three countries in West Africa where the economic analysis of the benefits have been completed, cassava green mite biological control with Z aripo has provided enorrnous economic benefits at no costtothefarmers: over$2.Zbillionfrom1983to2020 forBenin,GhanaandNigeria(Table1; Alene et a\.2005). In the remaining countries where cassava green mite biological control has been achieved similar benefits continue to be generated. Evaluation of the socioeconomic impact of this project in East and Southern Africa is underway.

triples.subject: spinosad
triples.source_sentence: A review by Bateman et al. (2018) on active ingre- dients registered for use against FAW indicates that spinosad is the widely used biopesticide in SSA. However, this must have been based on a very small sample size as by then many FAW plant protection products were still under evaluation on the conti- nent. If a survey was to be conducted now, it is likely that the most common active ingredient in FAW plant protection products would be emamectin benzoate (Chinwada, personal observation).

triples.subject: Africa Rising
triples.source_sentence: An SMS-based interactive service assisting farmers to prevent and mitigate FAW by acting appropriately to respond based on the severity, likely impact on the current crop, and cost-benefit.

triples.subject: AI-based Digital Monitoring System
triples.source_sentence: A digital monitoring system enabled by an app that leverages and deploys artificial intelligence (AI) to provide diagnoses and generate warning alerts for FAW outbreaks based on geographical spread and forecasting models.

triples.subject: Boa Me
triples.source_sentence: An artificial intelligence-powered, web-based application that combines past and satellite data, and user information about FAW and translates it into insights that farmers can access through local voice systems, SMS alerts, or a public announcement system.

triples.subject: CdPAS (Crop Disease & Pest Advisory Service)
triples.object: interactive voice response and smart app
triples.source_sentence: This combination of an interactive voice response and smart app allows farmers to report, predict, identify monitor and mitigate outbreak of FAW across Africa. It also provides crop disease prediction and advisory services, in addition to providing education and awareness through interactive voice response messaging in local languages.

triples.subject: Igeza
triples.source_sentence: A cloud-based mobile app enabling early detection of FAW via video, image or voice, with geolocation, which then sends all notifications to a pool of experts (entomologists, pathologists, agronomists etc.) to analyse the data and recommend appropriate control options.

triples.subject: CornBot
triples.object: audio-visual mobile maize disease diagnostic app
triples.source_sentence: An audio-visual mobile maize disease diagnostic app that interacts with farmers in their local languages to help them identify, track, map, and treat FAW.

triples.subject: FarmSmart FAW CONTROL
triples.source_sentence: An integrated image recognition app for FAW that links solution providers (researchers, manufacturers, and financial institutions) with farmers and allows paying a fraction of the control cost and rating the effectiveness of the solution provided.

triples.subject: Digicult
triples.source_sentence: A digital platform using mobile communication devices, multimedia processing, and crowdsourcing to analyse and share FAW data, and provide advice which helps farmers prevent and fight FAW.

triples.subject: EzyAgric
triples.source_sentence: A pest and disease diagnostic app, utilizing the EzyArmyWorm (EAW) module that allows farmers to detect FAW life stages, and predict yield loss.

triples.subject: Agri-Poll
triples.source_sentence: Smart survey platform that allows extension workers and key stakeholders to gather, analyse, and disseminate images (of pests and crops), location, time, weather, and environments in which the pests have been detected via feature phones, smart phones, and web platform.

triples.subject: FAWLEA: Pests? Problem solved!
triples.source_sentence: A mobile phone app that uses image recognition to detect and accurately identify FAW and the extent of crop damage, then provide the farmer with control options.

triples.subject: Desert Locust Guidelines
triples.source_sentence: A logical approach is required in order to avoid unnecessary, wasteful, dangerous and ineffective control operations.

triples.subject: Step 1
triples.source_sentence: Step 1. Decide whether control is necessary. This will depend on the type of target and where it is - see p. 4-5.

triples.subject: Step 2
triples.source_sentence: Step 2. If control is necessary, decide upon the scale and timing of the operation required. This will depend on factors such as how big the infestation seems to be, how urgent it is to get started and how quickly the infestation must be treated - see p. 4-5.

triples.subject: Step 3
triples.source_sentence: Step 3. Choose a control method, i.e. equipment, insecticide and technique. The method will depend on factors such as size of infestation and urgency, but also on what resources are available - see p. 6-33.

triples.subject: Step 4
triples.source_sentence: Step 4. Calibrate the control equipment so that the correct amount of insecticide is applied in the right way to the right place - see p. 34-45.

triples.subject: Step 5
triples.source_sentence: Step 5. Ensure that control will be safe to people and the environment - local populations should be informed so that they can move livestock, beehives and people away. Operators should use protective clothing and should identify and avoid sensitive ecological areas. See Safety and environmental precautions guideline for more details.

triples.subject: Step 6
triples.source_sentence: Step 6. Find and delimit the target, i.e. locate the locusts and mark the boundaries of the infestation - see p. 46-51.

triples.subject: Step 7
triples.source_sentence: Step 7. Check that weather conditions are suitable for the control method - see p. 52-53.

triples.subject: Step 8
triples.source_sentence: Step 8. Carry out the control - see p. 54-69.

triples.subject: Step 9
triples.source_sentence: Step 9. Monitor control operations and efficacy and record all relevant details for inclusion in a control report - see p. 70-79.

triples.subject: Step 10
triples.source_sentence: Step 10. Clean, service and store equipment. Store unused insecticides safely - see p. 80-81.

Like baiting, insecticide dusting has the advantage that it can be carried out without specialist application equipment - a hessian bag of dust beaten with a stick has commonly been used. triples.subject: Single hopper bands (spot treatment)
triples.source_sentence: Portable or vehicle-mounted sprayers can be used, but a lot of insecticide will be wasted with aircraft since they cannot be used efficiently for targets smaller than 0.25 km2 (25 ha).

triples.subject: Blocks of hopper bands
triples.source_sentence: This is wasteful of insecticide and has a greater potential environmental impact, but may be the only method fast enough to treat an area containing many bands before they fledge, i.e. become adults with wings.

triples.subject: Barrier spraying of hopper bands
triples.source_sentence: Barriers can be sprayed with a persistent insecticide in strips with large unsprayed areas in between. As the bands in the infested area move, they eventually encounter these sprayed strips and eat the sprayed vegetation.

triples.subject: ULV spraying
triples.source_sentence: The best time for spraying is usually in the morning between 0800 and 1100 hours and in the afternoon after 1600 hours. Effective spraying may be possible before 0800 hours if the wind is strong enough. It may also be possible to spray effectively between 1100 and 1600 hours if it is either cloudy and relatively cool (less than about 30 deg C) or if there is a steady wind over 4 m/s that will tend to prevent convection.

triples.subject: wind
triples.source_sentence: Never spray when there is no wind because the spray will not be spread properly over the swath and the operator is likely to be contaminated because the spray is not being carried away from him/her. There should be a steady wind of at least 2 m/s measured at a height of 2 m (a distinct breeze felt on the face). Do not spray when the wind is more than 10 m/s (dust and leaves are blown around) since it is not easy to predict where the spray will deposit.

triples.subject: sun
triples.source_sentence: Never spray when there is strong convection. Convection occurs when the sun rises high in the sky and heats up the ground. The hot ground warms up the air near to it, which then rises and may carry spray droplets out of the target area (see Fig. 21). Convection usually occurs on hot afternoons but may also occur in the late morning, especially if there is very little wind. Convection cannot usually be seen (except when strong updrafts pick up dust or if spray aircraft have smoke generators) but it can be detected by taking notice of wind strength and direction - frequent changes in wind strength and wind direction are a sure sign that convection is occurring.

triples.subject: rain
triples.source_sentence: Never spray if rain is falling or seems likely to fall soon, because the rain may wash off some of the insecticide from the vegetation.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: The efficacy of locust control should be assessed frequently during a control campaign.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: It does not have to be done accurately for every target, but spot checks should be made whenever possible, especially if new techniques or insecticides are being used.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: This has two purposes: to assess whether a repeat spray is required, and to check that insecticide and control technique are effective - if there are problems with the spraying, changes will have to be made before more (possibly ineffective) treatment is carried out.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: The assessment team needs to visit the target before spraying and some time afterwards to check it.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: This follow-up visit will usually be at the end of the spraying day or the following day, but timing of the efficacy assessment depends on the speed of action of the pesticide used and may be several days later.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: Even with excellent application, it is unrealistic to expect 100 percent locust mortality.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: There are many reasons for this including locusts being sheltered from the spray by vegetation or each other, locusts not feeding just before a moult and gaps in spray deposition due to localized air movements.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: In practice the objective should be at least 95 percent mortality.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: Most of the time, an exact percentage mortality is not required for bands or for swarms - if there are very few locusts remaining alive after spraying, there is no need to spend more time.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: However, if it is clear that a substantial number of locusts are not being killed by control operations, it may be necessary to estimate the percentage kill so that the failure can be reported properly and appropriate action taken.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: Even a rough estimate is often technically difficult because locusts can move out of the target area after spraying.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: This is especially true with slower-acting products which allow the locusts to move much further before they die.

triples.subject: pesticide
triples.source_sentence: There are also practical difficulties because the Locust Field Officers will probably be busy with other control operations in other areas on the following days.

triples.source_sentence: The spotted stem borer, Chilo partellus (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) is considered to be one of the devastating stem borer of sorghum and maize [4, 5] and also makes severe damage on rice in some African countries (Togola, unpublished data).

triples.subject: African striped rice borer
triples.source_sentence: The African striped rice borer, Chilo zacconius Bleszynski (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) is among the major rice stem borer species occurring in the humid forest and savanna zones according to Akinsola [6]. triples.subject: pink Stem Borer
triples.source_sentence: The pink Stem Borer Sesamia calamistis (Noctuidae) is generally less important than Busseola fusca and Chilo partellus as a pest of cereal crops in Africa but may be locally abundant. It attacks sorghum, maize, rice and sugarcane as main host. It can be found also on wheat and pearl millet.as secondary crop host and at less extend on wild grass such as Pennisetum purpureum, Setaria sp., Rottboellia exaltata and Cyperus distans as alternative host [10, 11].

triples.subject: millet stem borers
triples.source_sentence: The millet stem borers, Coniesta ignefusalis Hampson (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) is an important pest of pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum (L.) especially in West Africa [12]. The last generation enters diapause at the beginning of the dry season and stay for 6 months the time the next growing season comes.

triples.subject: Rice
triples.source_sentence: Rice is one of the major staple foods in Nigeria, consumed across all geopolitical zones and socioeconomic classes.

triples.subject: Rice
triples.source_sentence: However, rice production falls short of demand; the country depends heavily on rice importation of over 3 million tonnes annually, equivalent to over US$480 million in scarce foreign exchange.

triples.subject: Rice
triples.source_sentence: The Nigeria agricultural landscape is changing, with increased government policies aimed at stimulating private sector involvement and boosting local production.

triples.subject: Rice
triples.source_sentence: The efforts are starting to show results, as Nigeria's rice production rose from 3.7 million metric tonnes in 2017 to 4.0 million metric tonnes in 2018.

triples.subject: Rice
triples.source_sentence: Currently, most of the farmers producing rice rely on traditional technology with low use of improved input technologies.

triples.subject: Rice
triples.source_sentence: Average rice yields per unit area in the country are low and range between 2.0 and 3.0 t/ha compared to yields of 6 8 t/ha reported on research plots.

triples.subject: PLANT_POPULATION
triples.object: In dibbling or direct seeding, sow seeds 25 x 25 cm to give 160,000 stands/ha. Use a 'pinch' or 4 to 5 seeds paddy per hole. Plant about 3-5cm deep, cover lightly and press. In drilling method, drill in rows 15 - 20 cm apart.
triples.source_sentence: PLANT POPULATION In dibbling or direct seeding, sow seeds 25 x 25 cm to give 160,000 stands/ha. Use a 'pinch' or 4 to 5 seeds paddy per hole. Plant about 3-5cm deep, cover lightly and press. In drilling method, drill in rows 15 - 20 cm apart.

triples.subject: FERTILIZER_RATE
triples.object: BASAL FERTILIZER OR FIRST APPLICATION: Where basal fertilizer is applied, use phosphate and potash fertilizer in deficient soils at final harrowing before seeding. After bush burning, no phosphate and potash fertilizer are needed. Apply 100kg of 15-15-15 per hectare (2 bags/ha) as basal fertilizer or just at the time of first weeding (2 - 3 weeks after emergence) to facilitate incorporation of fertilizer into the soil. SECOND APPLICATION OF TOP DRESSING: Apply 50 kg (one bag) of Urea per hectare - 5 weeks after sowing. In areas where acidity is high, do NOT use Sulphate of Ammonia but use other sources of nitrogen e.g. urea.
triples.source_sentence: FERTILIZER RATE (i) BASAL FERTILIZER OR FIRST APPLICATION: Where basal fertilizer is applied, use phosphate and potash fertilizer in deficient soils at final harrowing before seeding. After bush burning, no phosphate and potash fertilizer are needed. Apply 100kg of 15-15-15 per hectare (2 bags/ha) as basal fertilizer or just at the time of first weeding (2 - 3 weeks after emergence) to facilitate incorporation of fertilizer into the soil. (ii) SECOND APPLICATION OF TOP DRESSING: Apply 50 kg (one bag) of Urea per hectare - 5 weeks after sowing. In areas where acidity is high, do NOT use Sulphate of Ammonia but use other sources of nitrogen e.g. urea.

entities.name: Oval spots with brown/light brown grey centres
Milled rice grains showing symptoms of infection
Transplant only seedlings that are healthy (free from brown spot symptoms)
Destroy volunteer rice crop and infected rice debris by burning soon after harvest
Control weeds in season and out of season
Amend soil with calcium silicate to boost resistance to the disease
Seed treatment: pre-soak seeds in cold water for 8 hours and treat with hot water (53-54 deg C) for 10-12 minutes before planting OR treat with fungicide for prevention before sowing
Monitor crop weekly through the season as disease can set in at all stages of growth
On the leaves and leaf sheaths look for small circular lesions, dark brown to purple in colour. Older lesions are more oval with a light brown to grey center surrounded by a reddish brown margin
Check glumes and panicle raches for dark brown to black oval spots or discoloration on the surface
Brown spot lesions can be mistaken for blast lesions
As soon as symptoms appear start control measures
Fungicides can also be applied as a preventative measure before the disease is seen
Rogue infected plants from the nursery to avoid disease spread and burn to destroy
Rogue plants with brown spot symptoms at low disease incidence in the field after transplanting
Mancozeb (e.g. Agrithane 80WP, Benco 80WP, Damazeb 80WP, Dizcozeb 80WP etc) at a rate of 75g/15L
Carbendazim (e.g. Carbendazim 50WP, Goldazim 500SC) at a rate of 25ml/15L

triples.source_sentence: The disease is spread more quickly in moist conditions such as during long periods of rain showers and absence of the sun. triples.subject: Sorghum
triples.source_sentence: Sorghum and millet cultivars include early, medium and late maturing types (Table 5). The greater the number of days to reach maturity, the taller the crop stands and the better the yield under good moisture, nutrient and temperature conditions. However, under arid conditions where moisture becomes more limiting, the early maturing cultivars will be more reliable to give good yields. Therefore the choice of maturity types will depend on prevailing conditions.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: Most determinate types are erect, that is they grow upright and do not need support.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: So, pods mature over a longer time and more than one harvest is required. Many of these types climb or creep along the ground.

triples.subject: Determinate cowpea varieties
triples.object: intercrop_with medium and late sorghum and millet varieties
triples.source_sentence: Since most of the determinate cowpea varieties on the market mature in around 60 days, it is good to intercrop them with medium and late sorghum and millet varieties to minimize competition for nutrients and sunlight.

triples.subject: Indeterminate cowpea varieties
triples.source_sentence: When using an indeterminate variety in an intercrop, it should not be allowed to climb the cereal plants, especially before the cereal heads emerge, to avoid shading.

triples.subject: Soybean
triples.source_sentence: Soybean has only recently started to be grown as an intercrop with sorghum or millet. Due to its longer maturity periods (almost 100 days), it is not commonly intercropped with these cereals.

triples.subject: germination_percentage
triples.source_sentence: the germination percentage can be calculated by dividing the number of well emerged or sprouted seeds by the initial number of seeds used and then multiply by 100: for example, if 25 seeds are used and 14 emerge/sprout then the germination percentage = (14/25) x 100 = 56%.

triples.subject: seed_treatment
triples.source_sentence: As well as low germination rates, farmers often also plant many seeds per hole because they want to compensate for the loss of seed through the feeding activities of soil-borne pests like ants and millipedes. Sometimes birds such as francolins dig up the seeds. Seed loss after planting can also be due to fungal infection already in the seed or present in the soil. In addition, seed may fail to germinate due to dormancy.

triples.subject: dormancy
triples.source_sentence: Sometimes sorghum and millet seed cannot germinate straight after harvesting due to a dormancy period. After the seed has been stored for about 3 months it germinates normally. Most pearl millet varieties do not show dormancy and can germinate after harvest. Dormancy is a useful trait when the crop is in the field because it ensures that the grains do not germinate on the heads if rained on. Dormancy can be broken by seed priming (see below).

triples.subject: Total cost of fertilizer per hectare

triples.subject: investment in fertilizer

triples.source_sentence: The first number is the percentage of the fertilizer that is N; the second number is the percentage of the fertilizer than supplies P; the third number is the percentage of the fertilizer that supplies K1 . So, the higher the number, the more of that nutrient the fertilizer supplies: for example, NPK 15-15-15 will supply more N, P and K per kg of fertilizer applied than NPK 17-17-17: NPK 15-15-15 will supply 150 g N while NPK 17-17-17 will supply 170 g N per kg of fertilizer.

triples.subject: Diammonium phosphate (DAP)
triples.source_sentence: Diammonium phosphate (DAP) supplies two of the three major plant nutrients, N and P.

triples.subject: Diammonium phosphate (DAP)
triples.source_sentence: DAP contains 18% N and 20% P (equivalent to 46% P2O5): one kg of DAP supplies 180 g of N and 200 g phosphorus (equivalent to 460 g of P2O5).

triples.subject: Urea
triples.source_sentence: Urea is a good example of a single nutrient, or straight fertilizer - urea only supplies the nutrient nitrogen (often abbreviated to N).

triples.subject: Urea
triples.source_sentence: Urea contains 46% nitrogen (N): one kg of urea therefore supplies 460 g of N but no phosphorus (P) or potassium (K).

triples.subject: Single superphosphate (SSP)
triples.source_sentence: Other examples of single nutrient fertilizers are single superphosphate (SSP; 20% P2O5) and triple superphosphate (TSP; 46% P2O5), both of which supply the nutrient phosphorus (P).

triples.subject: Triple superphosphate (TSP)
triples.source_sentence: Other examples of single nutrient fertilizers are single superphosphate (SSP; 20% P2O5) and triple superphosphate (TSP; 46% P2O5), both of which supply the nutrient phosphorus (P).

triples.subject: Organic matter
triples.source_sentence: As well as providing nutrients for plants, including N, P and K, organic matter also helps to maintain good soil health and structure: improving water retention and maintaining beneficial soil organisms such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms, amongst others.

triples.subject: Organic matter
triples.source_sentence: Farmers usually produce their own organic matter from their crops and livestock, but some may also buy them from neighbours or obtain them when neighbours' cattle, sheep and goats are allowed to graze their fields after harvest and deposit dung. Some farmers can harvest organic matter in the sylvo-pastoral lands (where there is open grassland and also trees and shrubs) or produce it through fallow systems.

triples.source_sentence: Mineral fertilizers are relatively expensive.

triples.subject: Zai pits
triples.source_sentence: Zai pits (Photo 4) are simple hand-dug holes which help to conserve water and contain higher levels of organic matter and nutrients that the surrounding soil. They are particularly useful for degraded soils and in regions where rainfall is poor and erratic. Zai pits improve infiltration of rain water and also capture runoff - in doing so they reduce soil erosion and importantly mitigate dry spells or drought.

triples.subject: Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM)
triples.object: A set of soil fertility management practices that necessarily include the use of fertilizer, organic inputs and improved germplasm combined with the knowledge on how to adapt these practices to local conditions, aiming at optimizing agronomic use efficiency of the applied nutrients and improving crop productivity. All inputs need to be managed following sound agronomic and economic principles.

triples.source_sentence: Sorghum can grow on different soils, but optimum grain and stover yields come from when grown on deep fertile, well-drained loamy soil. triples.subject: FYM
triples.source_sentence: For optimum yield, FYM application of 2 to 5 t/ha and well incorporated during land preparation is recommended. It helps in improving the soil structure, moisture retention capacity in drier areas as well as the nutrient content.

triples.subject: NPK 15:15:15

triples.subject: Urea

triples.subject: Organic (cow or sheep and goat dung)
triples.source_sentence: Micro-dose can also be done combining organic and inorganic fertilizers or with organic fertilizer alone. One hand full (100-200 g) of organic (cow or sheep and goat dung) per hill is sufficient.

triples.subject: Poultry manure
triples.source_sentence: Poultry manure could also be used in place of cow/sheep manure at the rate of 50-100 g per hill. Poultry manure has been found to contain more elemental fertilizer nutrients than ruminant manure.

triples.subject: African Army Worm
triples.object: occasional pest of sorghum in Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: The army worm (Spodoptera exempta Walker) is an occasional pest of sorghum in Nigeria.

triples.subject: African Army Worm
triples.source_sentence: The damage is caused by the larvae.

triples.subject: African Army Worm
triples.source_sentence: Major outbreaks can be controlled only if national or state organizations apply insecticides in outbreak areas.

triples.subject: Grasshoppers
triples.object: major pest, especially in the Sahel zone of Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: Grasshoppers (Oedalus senegalensis, Krauss) are a major pest, especially in the Sahel zone of Nigeria.

triples.subject: Grasshoppers
triples.source_sentence: Both nymphs and adults feed on sorghum as well as other cereals and wild grasses.

triples.subject: Grasshoppers
triples.source_sentence: It can be controlled by using insecticides.

triples.subject: Maize weevil
triples.object: most destructive insect pests of stored sorghum grain in Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: The weevil (Sitophilus zeamnis) and related species such as rice weevil (S. oryzzae) are the most destructive insect pests of stored sorghum grain in Nigeria.

triples.subject: Maize weevil
triples.source_sentence: Both adults and larvae feed on grain, which may often be damaged beyond use.

triples.subject: Maize weevil
triples.object: dry and clean condition, in insect proof containers
triples.source_sentence: Storing grains under dry and clean condition, in insect proof containers are some control measures.

triples.subject: Maize weevil
triples.source_sentence: If the grain moisture content is less than 9%, the insect is unable to feed. If keeping the grain dry is not practical, fumigation may be the only feasible protection.

triples.subject: Flour beetles
triples.source_sentence: The confused flour beetle (Tribolium confusum) and the flour beetle (T. castenum) are generally widely distributed.

triples.subject: Flour beetles
triples.object: larvae of T. confusum feed on flour or other materials such as grain dust and broken surfaces of grain kernels
triples.source_sentence: Larvae of T. confusum feed on flour or other materials such as grain dust and broken surfaces of grain kernels.

triples.subject: Flour beetles
triples.object: adult beetles of T. castenum construct tunnels when they move through flour or other granular products
triples.source_sentence: Adult beetles of T. castenum can readily be observed by the tunnels they construct when they move through flour or other granular products.

triples.subject: Flour beetles
triples.source_sentence: Storing products in sealed containers provides effective control.

triples.subject: Flour beetles
triples.source_sentence: Fumigants are also effective.

triples.subject: Stage 0
triples.source_sentence: 3 to 10 days after sowing, the plant begins to emerge. Growth is influenced by soil temperature and moisture, planting depth, and seed germination ability during emergence.

triples.subject: three - leaf stage
triples.source_sentence: The three - leaf stage occurs when the collars of three leaves can be seen without dissecting the plant. Depending on the temperature, this stage may occur approximately 10 days after emergence.

triples.subject: five - leaf stage
triples.source_sentence: The five - leaf stage occurs three weeks after emergence, when the collars of five leaves may be seen without dissecting the plant.

triples.subject: Growing Point Differentiation
triples.source_sentence: At this stage, the growing point of the sorghum plant changes from vegetative to reproductive. Nutrient uptake is rapid and adequate supplies of nutrients and water are necessary to achieve maximum growth. This stage occurs approximately 30 days after emergence and is about one third of the time from planting to physiological maturity.

triples.subject: Stage4. Boot Stage
triples.object: At this stage all the leaves are fully expanded, providing maximum leaf area and light interception. The head has reached full size and is encompassed by the flag-leaf sheath. Rapid growth and nutrient uptake continue. Stress from lack of moisture or via herbicide injury may prevent the head from emerging completely from the flag-leaf sheath preventing complete pollination at flowering.
triples.source_sentence: At this stage all the leaves are fully expanded, providing maximum leaf area and light interception. The head has reached full size and is encompassed by the flag-leaf sheath. Rapid growth and nutrient uptake continue. Stress from lack of moisture or via herbicide injury may prevent the head from emerging completely from the flag-leaf sheath preventing complete pollination at flowering.

triples.subject: Stage 5. Half Bloom
triples.object: This stage is defined as when half of the plants in a field have started to bloom. Flowering progresses from the tip of the head downward over a period of 4 to 9 days. Severe moisture stress can result in poor head filling.
triples.source_sentence: This stage is defined as when half of the plants in a field have started to bloom. Flowering progresses from the tip of the head downward over a period of 4 to 9 days. Severe moisture stress can result in poor head filling.

triples.subject: Stage 6. Soft Dough
triples.object: At this stage, the grain has a dough-like consistency and grain fill is occurring rapidly. The lower leaves continue to senesce with 8 to 12 leaves remaining at this stage.
triples.source_sentence: At this stage, the grain has a dough-like consistency and grain fill is occurring rapidly. The lower leaves continue to senesce with 8 to 12 leaves remaining at this stage.

triples.subject: Stage 7. Hard Dough
triples.object: By this stage approximately three-fourths of the grain dry weight has been attained. Nutrient uptake at this point is essentially complete. Severe moisture stress caused by an early freeze at this growth stage can result in light, chaffy grain.
triples.source_sentence: By this stage approximately three-fourths of the grain dry weight has been attained. Nutrient uptake at this point is essentially complete. Severe moisture stress caused by an early freeze at this growth stage can result in light, chaffy grain.

triples.subject: Stage 8. Physiological Maturity
triples.object: At this stage, the maximum total dry weight of the plant has been reached. This stage is marked by the appearance of a dark spot on the opposite side of the kernel from the embryo. Grain moisture at physiological maturity depends on the hybrid, with typical moisture ranging from 25% to 35%.

triples.subject: sorghum
triples.source_sentence: Sorghum cultivation is predominant in Northern Nigeria, where it is a traditional crop supporting the dietary needs of rural farmers for time immemorial. Sorghum provides food, fodder, raw material, and a source of cash income to rural farmers.

triples.subject: planting_date
triples.source_sentence: The planting date for garlic can be critical in northern Nigeria where garlic is mostly grown; it is recommended that garlic be planted between November and March during which the weather is cool.

triples.subject: recommended_varieties
triples.object: No distinct variety of garlic has so far been released in Nigeria, but many types are available with farmers across the country with varying characteristics such as size, shape, colour, yield, time of maturity, ease of bolting, pungency, storability, resistant to pest and diseases etc.
triples.source_sentence: No distinct variety of garlic has so far been released in Nigeria, but many types are available with farmers across the country with varying characteristics such as size, shape, colour, yield, time of maturity, ease of bolting, pungency, storability, resistant to pest and diseases etc. It is recommended that farmers should select varieties with desired qualities for plating.

triples.subject: seeds_preparation_and_treatment
triples.source_sentence: Before planting, detach the bulblets from the bulbs and soak in clean water for at least six (6) hours, then remove the outer skin from the bulblets and later drain the water and dries it with a mixture of fungicide and insecticide to control fungicides and seed attacking insects. These will enhance vigorous germination with minimal loss of seeds and seedlings.

triples.subject: method_of_planting
triples.source_sentence: Garlic can either be planted by dibbling, drilling or broadcasting. Dibbling method is mostly practiced and it consist of placing one clove per hole with the growing point upwards placed into the soil 3-6cm deep and 7 cm apart in rows of 15cm apart and cover lightly with soil.

triples.source_sentence: Bulb planting time: for true seed production bulb planting should be done during September to October months for flowering to take place between ends of December to early February. All the environmental factors required for seed production will be there for bulbs planted during September to October months.

triples.subject: Isolation
triples.source_sentence: Isolation: Onion is cross pollinated crop; seed field be isolated from other flowering type of onions by 500 - 1000 meters to avoid cross pollination by insects. Time isolation can also be used whenever possible. For bulb production 5-10 meters is required.

triples.subject: Land preparation
triples.source_sentence: Land preparation: the land be ploughed at least three times, the field be prepared well and ridges be made at 50 cm furrow distance including ridge.

triples.subject: Planting/spacing
triples.source_sentence: Planting/spacing: can be planted in double row or single row per ridge. In double row, mother bulbs are planted at 30 cm space between rows on a ridge and 20cm between plants on a row; this gives higher yield. Producers mostly use single row per ridge with a similar spacing (i.e. 50cm between rows and 20cm between plants) for ease of weeding and pesticides applications. However, when single row per ridge with similar spacing is used there is yield reduction that producers incur.

Onion
triples.source_sentence: Onion (Allium cepa) is a vegetable crop grown almost all over the world.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: It is grown mainly for its bulb, which is used in every home, almost daily.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Its main use lies in flavouring and seasoning of a wide variety of dishes.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Its popularity is due to its aromatic, volatile oil, the allyl-prophl sulphide which imports a cherished flavour to food.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: As a constituent of a meal, both the green leaves and bulbs can be eaten raw, cooked or flood, or in soups and salads.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Onion also has an important role as a medicinal herb in many communities, and is claimed to minimize high blood pressure and other heart diseases due to its favourable action on the elasticity of blood vessels.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: As an item of world trade, onion ranks second in importance after tomatoes among the vegetables.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: In 1987, the total world export production amounted to over 2.0 million metric tones and worth over 299 million US dollars.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: World production of onion has increased steadily from about 11 million metric tones produced on an area of nearly 0.9 million hectare in 1969 to over 25 million metric tones produced on an area of above 1.7 million hectares in 1987.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: These figures represent and percent increases in total production and at as respectively.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Onion is grown widely during the wet and dry seasons.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: However yields are much higher during the dry season because of fewer incidences of pests and diseases.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Prices of onion tend to oxalate during the dry season before harvest begins, due largely to the inability of the farmers to store the highly perishable crop.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Dry season production of onion is on the increase due to the provision of more irrigation facilities.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Although onion has been grown in Nigeria for a long time, the yield is still low compared to other regions of the world.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: The reason for this is because improved production practices based on research findings have not been made available to the generality of farmers.

triples.subject: Fertilizer_Recommendation

For general purposes however, a fertilizer rate of 65 kg N/ha - 40kg p/ha and 45kg k/ha, that is about 6 bags of NPK 15:15:15 and 1 and half bag of urea commended.

triples.subject: Pests_and_Diseases
triples.source_sentence: The common insect pests that affect onions are thrips (Thrips tabaci Lind), onion maggot (Hylemya antiqua Meig), and sea corn maggot (Hylemya cilicrura (Rondani) salt marsh caterpillar (Estigmene acred Drurn), wireworms of the genus limonius, cutworms of the family Noctuidapea leaf miner (Liriomiza langei Frick) and several species of mites.

triples.subject: Pests_and_Diseases
triples.source_sentence: These are pests of onion that causes serious damage to an onion crop, particularly at the beginning of the season, both in the nursery beds and after transplanting in the field.

triples.subject: Pests_and_Diseases
triples.source_sentence: The larvae of the moth eat the leaves of onion and can sometimes be serious.

triples.subject: Pests_and_Diseases
triples.source_sentence: Both the larvae and adult thrips cause damage. They feed on the contents if leaf epidermal cell, which then become air filled to give a silvery appearance. Infested leaves of older plants may become distorted while younger onion plants may be killed.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Onions are generally harvested by hand pulling. They are then laid on their sides for a number of days for further ripening in the open. If they do not lie on their sides, they tend to take root in wet weather and start growing again.

triples.subject: Onion
triples.source_sentence: Before onion bulbs are placed in storage or marketed, the tops are usually removed and frequently also the roots. Removal of the tops, especially of the necks are not dry, provides an open, moist surface where not organisms can easily enter. These neck tissues, and all other moist surface tissue of the bulb where not organisms might become established, should be carefully dried before infection can occur. This drying procedure is known as curing. In areas where the relative humidity is low and rains seldom occur during the harvest season, curing is easily and effectively done in the field storage.

triples.subject: transplanting_spacing
triples.source_sentence: Peppers, like many other vegetable crops, require a reasonably uniform soil - moisture supply during the growing season for best production. Long dry period may cause shedding of flowers and young fruits, and the plants are likely to make a rather slow recovery after drought injury. The most popularly used systems are basin and furrow irrigation system. Peppers are estimated to require between 600 - 800mm of water per season.

triples.subject: transplanting_spacing
triples.source_sentence: Peppers, like many other vegetable crops, require a reasonably uniform soil - moisture supply during the growing season for best production. Long dry period may cause shedding of flowers and young fruits, and the plants are likely to make a rather slow recovery after drought injury. The most popularly used systems are basin and furrow irrigation system. Peppers are estimated to require between 600 - 800mm of water per season. An average of 15 to 20 irrigations are required to produce a crop of peppers depending on when irrigation season starts.

triples.subject: transplanting_spacing
triples.source_sentence: An example of the chemicals used to control weeds in plant beds is methyl bromide. Prepare the soil as for seeding, omitting the final smoothing or compaction operation. Cover the area to be treated with an airtight plastic film. triples.source_sentence: Cutworms can be controlled by applying toxaphene as a dust or spray to the plants and to the soil around their bases at the rate of 2.268kg per hectare. triples.source_sentence: The European corn borer, Pyraustanubilalis (Hubner), has become a serious pest of peppers grown.

triples.subject: Flea Beetles
triples.source_sentence: Flea beetles, Exitrix spp, are small, black, brown, or striped Jumping beetles (fig.12). They damage peppers wherever this plant is grown.

triples.subject: Hornworms
triples.source_sentence: The tomato hornworms Protoparce quinquemaculate (Hawarth), and the tobacco hornworm, P.sexta (Johanson), are large green worms with diagonal lines along the sides and a prominent horn on the rear end (fig. 13). They devour the leaves of pepper plants and when numerous may entirely strip them.

triples.subject: Thiram
triples.source_sentence: Treating pepper seed with certain fungicides to protect the young seedlings until they emerge from the soil can reduce losses from damping - off. This material includes preparations of such chemical as thiram. It should be used at the rate recommended by the manufacturers.

triples.subject: Captan
triples.source_sentence: Damping - off in the seedbed (or fields) can be checked immediately after planting the seed by wetting the soil with a suspension of 2kg of captan to 455litres of water applied as a spray. This is applied at the rate of 4.5litres to each 11.6 square metre of soil.

triples.subject: ICS-Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: In recent past, investment in the support services to Nigerian agriculture has been neglected with the result that this sector has not realized its full potential to contribute to the prosperity and economic development of the country.

triples.subject: ICS-Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: Meanwhile, increasing population pressure and the accompanying need to intensify agricultural production is leading to erosion of the natural resource base on which agriculture depends.

triples.subject: ICS-Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: The sustainability of production is threatened by a vicious cycle of declining soil fertility and increasing problems of pests, diseases, and weeds.

triples.subject: ICS-Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: The sustainability of production is threatened by a vicious cycle of declining soil fertility and increasing problems of pests, diseases, and weeds.

triples.subject: ICS-Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: Moreover, the lack of knowledge on how to add value through proper storage, processing, and marketing impedes agricultural growth.

triples.subject: ICS-Nigeria
triples.source_sentence: Promising technologies exist to address these problems, but their adoption is constrained by a lack of information packaged in appropriate formats, and poor communication channels for this information, between farmers and the research, extension, and education organizations that are supposed to address these issues.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: As part of its contribution to the economic recovery process in the North East Part of Nigeria which has been ravaged by the insurgent activities of armed groups, USAID awarded to the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) and its Partners (International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics and Catholic Relief Services) the two-year "Feed the Future Nigeria Integrated Agriculture Activity'' which aims to advance the objectives of inclusive and sustainable agriculture-led economic growth; strengthened resilience among people and systems; and a well-nourished population, especially among women and children in targeted locations of Borno and Adamawa states, Nigeria. The Activity seeks to support vulnerable populations to engage in basic farming activities that will improve food security, increase agricultural incomes and improve resilience among smallholder farmers and their families. It works with a coalition of partners to facilitate improved agro-inputs and extension advisory services to serve vulnerable populations;

triples.source_sentence: Planting date affects cowpea seed yield and quality. It also affects the use of insecticides for controlling insect pests.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: High yields of good quality seeds are obtained when cowpea is planted so that the crop matures in dry weather.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: For the photoperiod-sensitive cowpea to flower early, these varieties should, therefore, be planted from late- July to mid-August when the daylength is becoming shorter, depending on the amount and distribution of rainfall.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: On the other hand, the erect type, early and medium maturing varieties that are photoperiod-insensitive can be planted at any time in the year, provided rainfall is sufficient, or there are irrigation facilities.

triples.subject: Cowpea

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: Plant types are often categorized as erect, semi-erect, prostrate (trailing), or climbing.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: There is much variability within the species.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: Growth habit ranges from indeterminate to fairly determinate with the non-vining types tending to be more determinate.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: These varieties respond differently to different photoperiods and growing environments.

triples.subject: Cowpea
triples.source_sentence: The most damaging flowering insect pests of cowpea are thrips, (Megalurothrips sjostedti Trybom.) and Maruca. They are frequently responsible for total crop loss.

triples.subject: Thrips
triples.source_sentence: Attack during the pre-flowering period may damage the terminal leaf bud and bracts, causing the latter to become deformed with a brownish-yellow appearance.

triples.subject: Thrips
triples.source_sentence: The pest feeds on flower buds and flowers.

triples.subject: Thrips

triples.subject: Thrips

triples.subject: Thrips

triples.subject: Thrips
triples.source_sentence: Yield losses from this insect pest have been estimated at between 20 and 100%.

triples.subject: Thrips

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: Among the cowpea pod borers, Maruca vitrata is the most widespread. It is a pre- and post-flowering pest and feeds on every part of the plant.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: The adult is a nocturnal moth, light brown with whitish markings on its forewings, and lays eggs on the plant.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: The larvae that emerge damage plants in the field, particularly during the reproductive stage, through feeding on the tender parts of the stems, peduncles, flower buds, flowers, pods, and seeds.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: The holes bored on the buds, flowers, or pods by feeding are the damage symptom.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: Infested pods and flowers are webbed together.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: This pest can cause a significant grain yield reduction of between 20 and 80% if not controlled with insecticides.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: Complete crop failure may occur, especially in situations where management strategies are not applied.

triples.subject: Maruca vitrata
triples.source_sentence: No good sources of resistance have been found within the cowpea genotypes. See Table 7 for a list of chemical insecticides to control this pest.

triples.subject: insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Insecticides are toxic to both pests and humans. If used improperly, insecticides can poison people, pets, and livestock. They can also damage beneficial insects, birds, fish, and other wildlife, harm desirable plants, and may contaminate soil and groundwater. Some of the precautions that must be taken during transport, storage, and handling of insecticides are highlighted below.

triples.subject: insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Pesticides should be stored in a safe, secure, and well-identified place that is not accessible to unauthorized people or children. Insecticides should never be kept in a place where they might be mistaken for food or drink. Keep them dry but away from fires and out of direct

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Insecticides must be stored in tightly-sealed containers.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Make sure that storage areas for insecticides are well-ventilated to prevent the accumulation of toxic fumes.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Always store different types of insecticides in different areas, to prevent cross-contamination and the possibility of inadvertently applying a product.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Never store pesticides in old bottles or food containers where they could be mistaken for food or drink for humans or animals.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Insecticides are most safely transported in the beds of trucks.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: They should never be transported in the passenger compartment of any vehicle nor in the same compartment as food, feed, or clothing.

triples.subject: Insecticides

triples.subject: Insecticides

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: Left-over insecticide suspension can be safely discarded by being poured into a pit latrine or a hole in the ground, dug especially at least 100 m away from streams, wells, and houses.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: It should not be unloaded where it may enter water used for drinking or washing, fish ponds, or rivers.

triples.subject: Insecticides
triples.source_sentence: In hilly areas, the holes should be dug on the lower slopes.

triples.subject: Protective_clothing
triples.source_sentence: Spray workers should wear overalls or shirts with long sleeves and trousers, a broad-brimmed hat, a turban or other headgear, and sturdy shoes or boots.

triples.subject: Protective_clothing
triples.source_sentence: The mouth and nose should be covered with a simple device such as a disposable paper mask, a surgical-type disposable or washable mask, or any clean piece of cotton.

triples.subject: Protective_clothing
triples.source_sentence: The cotton should be changed if it becomes wet.

triples.subject: Protective_clothing
triples.source_sentence: The clothing should be of cotton for ease of washing and drying.

triples.subject: Protective_clothing

triples.subject: Protective_clothing
triples.source_sentence: In hot and humid climates, the wearing of additional protective clothing may be uncomfortable, and pesticides should, therefore, be applied during the cooler hours of the day.

triples.subject: GRD
triples.source_sentence: GRD is a virus disease, transmitted by an aphid, Aphis craccivora Koch (Insecta: Homoptera) (Storey and Bottomley 1928; Storey and Ryland 1955, 1957; Hull and Adams 1968).

triples.subject: GRD
triples.source_sentence: Three causal agents are involved in GRD etiology: Groundnut rosette assistor virus (GRAV), Groundnut rosette virus (GRV) and a Satellite-RNA (SatRNA) (Reddy et al. 1985a,b; Murant et al. 1988; Taliansky et al. 2000).

triples.subject: GRD
triples.source_sentence: An epidemic in northern Nigeria in 1975 destroyed approximately 0.7 million ha of groundnut, with an estimated loss of US$250 million (Yayock et al. 1976).

triples.subject: GRD
triples.source_sentence: Similarly, an epidemic in 1995 in eastern Zambia affected approximately 43,000 ha causing an estimated loss of US$4.89 million.

triples.subject: GRD
triples.source_sentence: As per the estimates of ICRISAT, GRD causes an annual yield loss of US$156 million in SSA.

triples.subject: GRAV
triples.source_sentence: The virus on its own causes symptomless infection or transient mottle, and can cause significant yield loss in susceptible groundnut cultivars (Naidu et al. 2007).

triples.source_sentence: During short inoculation feeding (test probe or stylet pathway phase) vector aphids probe groundnut leaves without reaching the phloem, transmitting only GRV and SatRNA, which multiply in the epidermal and mesophyll cells.

triples.subject: Vector aphids

triples.subject: Groundnut Rosette Virus (GRV)
triples.source_sentence: Monitor young plants weekly for aphids vectors. Examine leaf surfaces after germination particulary growing tips - aphids prefer feeding on young and soft tissue.

triples.subject: Groundnut Rosette Virus (GRV)
triples.source_sentence: Look for glossy black or dark brown bodied aphids measuring about 2 mm in length on the plants.

triples.subject: Groundnut Rosette Virus (GRV)
triples.source_sentence: Monitor young plants from 30-45 days after sowing for symptoms of rosette - stunted growth, chlorosis and reduced leaf sizes and leaf distortion.

triples.subject: Groundnut Rosette Virus (GRV)
triples.source_sentence: Start control as soon as symptoms of the virus are observed or the presence aphids are detected.

triples.subject: Weed control
triples.source_sentence:
Manual weed control
Carry out the first weeding at 2 weeks after planting and the second at 5 - 6 weeks after planting. Avoid weeding immediately after rainfall as this would lead to transplanting the weeds. Poor hoe weeding or delay in weeding could cause significant reductions in soybean yields.

triples.subject: Weed control
triples.source_sentence:
Chemical weed control
Herbicides, if used properly, are safe and effective in controlling weeds in soybean. The choice, however, depends on the predominant weed species and the availability of the herbicide. Herbicides are available for pre-emergence or post-emergence weed control. If the herbicide is applied at planting, one weeding may be required at 5 - 6 weeks after planting. Use herbicides as presented in Table 4.

triples.subject: Cypermethrin + Dimethoate 10 EC
triples.source_sentence:
Insect pests and their control
Several different insects occur in soybean fields but few are of any economic importance, and the species that cause damage are usually not abundant enough to make control measures necessary. In the vegetative stage, the crop is very tolerant of caterpillars but very susceptible to attacks by silverleaf whiteflies. From flowering stage onwards, soybean becomes attractive to pod-sucking bugs that can seriously reduce seed quality. Insect pests can be controlled with a single spray of Cypermethrin + Dimethoate 10 EC at the rate of 100 mL in 15 L of water.

From flowering stage onwards, soybean becomes attractive to pod-sucking bugs that can seriously reduce seed quality. Insect pests can be controlled with a single spray of Cypermethrin + Dimethoate 10 EC at the rate of 100 mL in 15 L of water.
